The verdict came at four in the afternoon. Guilty on all counts. The courtroom went silent. The defendant stared straight ahead. His attorney placed a hand on his shoulder. In the gallery, the victim's family held each other. No celebration. Just relief -- quiet and exhausted. The trial lasted eleven days. The prosecution presented forensic evidence, surveillance footage, and testimony from three eyewitnesses. The defense argued misidentification. The jury did not buy it. They deliberated for six hours. Justice, in this case, worked the way it is supposed to. But that is not always the story. Across the country, thousands of cases sit untried. Evidence kits gather dust in storage rooms. Witnesses move away or lose faith. The system works -- when it works. The problem is how often it does not. One verdict does not fix a broken process. It just proves the process can function when given the resources it needs.
